source.title: MetaSAEs: Joint Training with a Decomposability Penalty Produces More Atomic Sparse Autoencoder Latents

page_placements.theme: Feature composition and cross-method granularity at a fixed dictionary size

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether a different SAE training objective changes feature atomicity, using co-occurrence and automated interpretability measures plus qualitative feature-split examples. It does not sweep dictionary size.
record.gate_note: The study compares solo and jointly trained SAEs with the same primary dictionary size; it does not test increasing dictionary size or directly measure whether split features have nearby decoder directions or partition all of a parent feature's inputs. The cited Einstein example is from prior work, not a result of this study. Reconstruction-cost results are not rows because they do not measure the claim's splitting or atomicity outcomes.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It adds a meta-SAE decomposability penalty and reports its own method against a solo SAE at a fixed dictionary size (20,480 on GPT-2 large; 65,536 on Gemma 2 9B). The measures are mean |φ| co-occurrence, fuzzing scores and cross-SAE splitting examples. No result measures how features split as the dictionary grows (V1/V2), hierarchical families (V3), absorption (V4), or larger-vs-smaller dictionary composition (V5). The paper builds on Bussmann et al.'s meta-SAE non-atomicity finding without retesting it. It also never measures whether splitting comes from the sparsity objective (V6). Its 'splits' are differences between two objectives at the same size, not splitting with dictionary size. The rows compare the study's own method with a baseline, so they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that joint training with a meta-SAE decomposability penalty yields more atomic latents. On GPT-2 large this means −7.5% mean |φ| and +7.6% fuzzing, at +0.6 percentage points of CE overhead over the solo SAE. Gemma 2 9B results (+8.6% ΔFuzz) are directional, and qualitative cases show blended features separated into sense-specific ones. The authors also state that λ2=1.0 fails.
record.recipe_differences: The study adds a simultaneously trained meta SAE and a decomposability penalty to primary SAE training; it does not compare dictionaries of increasing size.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with λ2 and σ2: λ2 = 1.0 worsens mean |φ|, while λ2 ∈ {0.1, 0.3} gives reductions on GPT-2 large. Gemma's co-occurrence scan is reported as small and mixed, and its scan uses fewer evaluation tokens than the GPT-2 scan.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed dictionary size, a meta-SAE decomposability penalty lowers within-SAE co-occurrence on GPT-2 large L20 (best −7.5% mean |φ|). At λ2=1.0, |φ| rises instead (+2.6 to +3.8%), and the λ2=0 control shows no effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Changing the SAE training objective at a fixed dictionary size changes latent co-occurrence (atomicity), with an optimum at moderate penalty strength.

fits_no_version.finding: The jointly trained SAE gets higher fuzzing scores than the solo SAE: +7.6% on GPT-2 large (p=5e-16) and a directional +8.6% on Gemma 2 9B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decomposability-penalised SAEs yield more interpretable latents by automated fuzzing.

fits_no_version.finding: Polysemous solo-SAE latents ('too', 'let', 'cookies', 'flash') co-occur with several sense-specific latents in a same-size SAE trained with the penalty. This is a cross-objective analogue of splitting, not a size-driven one.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At equal dictionary size, a different training objective can separate a blended latent into several sense-specific latents.

record.problems: Only one layer is evaluated per model. Gemma SAEs are not fully converged, and the Gemma co-occurrence scan is described as underpowered with wide confidence intervals. Qualitative split examples do not quantify how completely child features partition parent inputs or directly measure the proximity of their decoder directions.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results were omitted. Reconstruction L2 and language-model CE costs are not rows because they do not measure feature splitting or atomicity.

untested.parts: No dictionary-size sweep. Coarse-to-fine splitting, coverage of the parent's inputs, and decoder proximity are not measured.
No size sweep on GPT-2 large or Gemma 2 9B, and no open SAE releases are evaluated.
Nested feature families and their geometric correspondence to a concept hierarchy are not tested.
Absorption (a parent failing to fire where a child does), and whether size or sparsity fixes it, are not measured.
Larger-vs-smaller SAE decomposition and novel latents are not tested. The meta-SAE non-atomicity finding is cited from Bussmann et al., not retested.

Whether splitting with dictionary size is produced by the sparsity objective on hierarchical or correlated inputs is not tested. Matryoshka SAEs are not tested. Splitting under the new objective is not compared across dictionary sizes.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 and its V2/V6 labels are rejected. The study's 'splitting' is a solo-vs-joint comparison at identical dictionary size, which is the study's own method against a baseline. It neither tests size-driven splitting nor whether splitting is an objective artifact. The cited Einstein meta-SAE example is prior work (Bussmann et al. 2024).

versions.untested_parts: No dictionary-size sweep or comparison of coarse features across increasing dictionary sizes.
Open SAE releases are not evaluated. The study uses one layer per model and does not establish generality across many models or layers; Gemma results are described as directional.
No test of nested feature families or whether their geometry mirrors a hierarchy of concepts in the model.
No measurement of parent-latent firing where a child fires, absorption, or whether changing SAE size or sparsity resolves absorption.
No comparison of larger and smaller SAE dictionaries for latent combinations or novel latents.

The study tests a decomposability penalty's effect on atomicity-related outcomes, but does not test whether ordinary SAE splitting is an artifact of the sparsity objective on correlated or hierarchical inputs, whether it reflects the model's own units, or Matryoshka SAEs.

relation.reason: It uses meta-SAE decomposability and cross-SAE splitting candidates as tools for its own method. It does not test any version. The reader's guess of tests/T2 is not supported.

tranche.reason: This is a methods paper. It reports its own decomposability-penalty method against a solo SAE at a fixed dictionary size, and it has no dictionary-size sweep.

source_check.notes: All six rows match the text. The qualitative splits compare the solo and joint objectives at the same size (GPT-2 large 20,480; Gemma 2 9B 65,536), not splitting as the dictionary grows. The authors call the Gemma results directional. The solo CE overhead is 2.4% in the Table 1 caption but 2.5% in Sec 5.3.

statements.correction: GPT-2 large L20 (20,480 latents): best -7.5% mean |phi| at lambda2=0.3, sigma2=1.0. lambda2=1.0 gives +2.6 to +3.8%. The lambda2=0 control shows no systematic effect. 'too' and 'let' are GPT-2 large L20 cases. 'cookies' and 'flash' are Gemma 2 9B layer 23 cases (65,536 latents, results the authors call directional). Each split compares the solo and penalised SAE at the same size. 'flash' splits into 2 joint latents (63365, 34102).
statements.problem: The numbers are right for GPT-2 large L20. But the statement is scoped to 'GPT-2 large L20' and lists 'cookies' and 'flash' among the solo latents. Those two cases come from Gemma 2 9B layer 23.
